children: By Jen Rose Smith | Photography by Dayyan Armstrong for WSJ
Brackish water dripped down Anna Drzewiecki's arm as she showed me a palm-sized oyster she had just pulled from a cage at Glidden Point Oyster Farms on Maine's Damariscotta River.

"As close to the source as it gets," said Drzewiecki, who was leading a $26 hourlong tour of the site. Away from the dock, I sat down with a tray of oysters and a stabby, plastic-handled knife. The bounty came not just from Glidden's 40-acre oyster operation, where the shellfish grow in cages on the Damariscotta's surface and bottom, but from neighbors up and down the river.

Aquaculture farms can be found all along Maine's coastline, with an official Maine Oyster Trail linking many of the stops along the way. But the greatest concentration of farms is along the 19-mile tidal Damariscotta, the site of oyster feasts for thousands of years.

For travelers on a tight timeline, a quick trip around the Damariscotta is a chance to sample the best of a state where oysters reach peak flavor just as summer crowds disperse. In just two days on the road, I tried to cover as much ground as possible.
At Glidden, the first stop on my trip, the oysters had the umami tang of chicken soup. A dribble of mignonette barely tamed their muscular salinity.

The night before, I had whet my appetite at the Parlor, a four-seat oyster bar in nearby Bath. There, certified oyster sommelier Virginia Shaffer explained what makes Damariscotta oysters so good: cold clean water, a silty river bottom and a salt pond that feeds the river, functioning like an all-you-can-eat buffet for growing bivalves.

"There's something really special in the water," said Shaffer. Her company, Lady Oyster, takes travelers on tours of oyster farms. Gradations in minerals, current and temperature along the Damariscotta mean each farm's oysters taste a little different. "It's just this unfiltered taste of place," she said.

Glidden is one of the oldest farms on the Damariscotta, among a handful that were started in the 1970s and '80s-decades after the wild oysters that had grown in the area had been choked out by industry. Another farm established late last century was Pemaquid Oyster Company, whose co-founder, Smokey McKeen, met me for midday beers at the riverside seafood restaurant Schooner Landing, after my visit to Glidden.

When McKeen's company started farming oysters in 1986, most chefs thought the shellfish came in a can, he said. McKeen recalled how he and other farmers at the time would pitch restaurants on serving fresh oysters, while simultaneously developing a scrappy style of aquaculture to propagate them in the Damariscotta.
"We were literally broadcasting seed oysters over the side of our boats," McKeen said, referring to the way they would distribute juvenile oysters across the river bottom. It worked.

Later that day, Chip Holmes, co-owner of Damariscotta River Cruises, told me that a dozen Damariscotta farms now produce 80% of Maine oysters. We were aboard an open-sided boat that Holmes was steering past some of the river's farms.
During his $45 two-hour tours that embark from a dock at Schooner Landing, Holmes offers a steady patter of oyster-related wisecracks, as his partner, Olga Oros, shucks and hands out shellfish.

The oysters from Heron Island, a one-man operation in Fitch Cove about three miles downstream from Schooner Landing, tasted of grass-fed butter. The varieties from Pemaquid Oyster Company started with a salty brine that teed up an oceanic kick of kelp. As the oysters kept coming, I kept eating them.

This level of gluttony is nothing new on the Damariscotta. The area is littered with massive piles of shells called middens, left by indigenous groups who ate the river's wild oysters for more than a thousand years. The next morning, I followed a lupine-lined walking trail to one of the biggest piles, Whaleback Shell Midden, which was once estimated at 45 million cubic feet-enough shells to bury a Manhattan block 20 stories high.

Recently, the area's wild oysters started reappearing: A University of Maine study published last year noted their resurgence in midcoast Maine. Climate change likely plays a role, since they prefer warmer water, but the farmed oysters introduced in the 1970s and '80s may have helped by cleaning up the river.

Genetic evidence suggests the wild oysters are their offspring-spawn that slipped the cages and grew free. Their number pales in comparison to that of farm-raised oysters on the Damariscotta, which remain the main draw.

For my final shellfish meal, I joined the evening crowd at the Shuck Station, a seasonal restaurant in a former gas station owned by Brendan Parsons. He is also the owner of Blackstone Point Oysters, a farm near Whaleback Shell Midden.
"This was a sacred place where so many Native Americans came together to share food," Parsons said of the area.

At the Shuck Station, I joined the evening crowd dining at its outdoor picnic tables. The house oysters, Blackstone Points, had a seaweed whiff and creamy aftertaste; heftier Pleasant Cove Oysters were the briniest of the 11 types I had on my trip.
At the next picnic table over, a little girl tipped an oyster back then dropped it on the ground-one more shell for the modern midden.
What to know before you go
You can slurp your way along the Damariscotta at any time of year. But timing still matters; here's what to know.
Go now

September kicks off what many consider to be the tastiest season, said Glidden Point's Anna Drzewiecki. "The oysters have a robust flavor," she said, because the bivalves are storing fat and sugar for winter, resulting in crowd-pleasing meat-to-shell ratios. While Glidden harvests oysters even when ice forms on the Damariscotta, its tours run only through mid-October.
Order in

Some Damariscotta operations, including Norumbega Oyster Inc and Glidden Point offer overnight shipping year-round. Brendan Parsons of the Shuck Station says cold months have better oysters-winter ones are salty, mineral-crisp and firm.
Shuck convention

Old wisdom claims that you should only eat oysters in months with names that contain the letter R. But from May to August, peak travel season on the coast, waterside oyster bars crank out shucked bivalves that are soft, buttery and still delicious. "There's never a wrong time to sit at the beach and eat oysters," Parsons said.
